activities.anchor: the training session itself makes you
activities.caption: the arc of one session — put the phases in order
activities.name: tlaSessionOrder

config.prompt: One training session, from stimulus to stimulus — order the arc:
items: The hard session — straight afterwards you are slower, weaker and stiffer than before you started
Days of eating, sleeping and easy movement — the body repairs the damage
The over-rebuild: preparing for the next assault by raising the ceiling — supercompensation
Time the next session onto the peak of the last one's recovery curve
config.why: Training doesn't make you fitter; training plus recovery does — the exercise is only the stimulus, the way a question is only the stimulus for an answer.

activities.anchor: Worked example: a novice runner does a hard 5 km on Monday.
activities.caption: pick her next hard day — the curve decides
activities.name: tlaTimingBranch

config.root: A novice runner does a hard 5 km on Monday. The question is when she trains hard next.

start.text: The Monday session is in the legs. She scans the week for the next hard run.

choices.label: Tuesday — ride the momentum
choices.feedback: Tuesday she feels leaden — that is the dip. Hard work now stacks fatigue onto fatigue: the road to overtraining.

choices.label: Thursday — the same pace feels lighter
choices.feedback: Days 3–5 are the window of elevated capacity — each wave started here begins higher than the last.

choices.label: Sunday — play it safe with a long gap
choices.feedback: Too late: the adaptation has faded. The curve was there and she trained beside it.

stacked.text: Fatigue on fatigue — performance drifts down instead of up. Only a recovery block resets the curve.

peak.text: The next session lands on the peak: the same work now starts from a higher ceiling.

faded.text: The window closed days ago — the same work, but none of Monday's adaptation left to build on.

config.why: Get the timing wrong in either direction and the same work produces either injury or nothing.

activities.anchor: A sumo wrestler is extraordinarily fit for his sport
activities.caption: two words that are not synonyms — drag the divider
activities.name: tlaHfCompare

config.prompt: The same athlete, read two ways — drag the divider:

before.label: fitness
before.text: the ability to meet the demands of an environment or a task — task-shaped and partly negotiable: the sumo wrestler is extraordinarily fit for his sport

after.label: health
after.text: complete physical, mental and social well-being — whole-person and not negotiable: the same wrestler may have hypertension; a marathon runner with a racing heart rate can still be depressed

config.why: More fitness generally improves health — but you can chase fitness in ways that damage it: under-eating, overtraining, doping.

activities.caption: scrub the first two minutes — the systems hand over in sequence
activities.name: tlaFuelTimeline

events.title: all-out effort begins
events.text: The ATP–phosphocreatine system powers sprints and lifts — fuel already stored in the muscle.

events.title: first handover
events.text: The anaerobic (lactic) system takes over: burning glucose without oxygen — the burn of hard effort.

events.title: the aerobic system takes the wheel
events.text: Beyond about two minutes: carbohydrate and fat burned with oxygen — a 5 km run, and everything longer.

config.prompt: A 70 kg athlete in hard training spreads protein across the day. Roughly how many grams per day does the lesson's range imply?
config.why: Roughly 1.4–2.0 g per kg of body mass × 70 kg ≈ 100–140 g — construction needs materials, and you cannot supercompensate on an empty site.

activities.anchor: lactic acid from a hard session sits in the muscles
activities.caption: one line of this explanation is wrong — find it
activities.name: tlaLactateSpot

config.prompt: This account of next-day soreness contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: During the 400 m race the burn was real: the anaerobic system burns glucose without oxygen.
After stopping, the lactate is largely cleared or consumed as fuel within about an hour.
The soreness arriving a day or two later is caused by lactate still sitting in the muscles.
The late soreness comes from repair processes around micro-damage, so it tracks novelty to the muscle.
Endurance training teaches the body to reuse lactate — less a poison than a shuttle.
config.correction: Lactate does not sit in the muscles until the next day — it is cleared within about an hour; the late soreness belongs to the repair, not the burn.
config.why: It is an appealing story — the burn was there, the soreness came later — but cause and effect is exactly what it lacks.

activities.caption: file the components before programming them
activities.name: tlaCompSort

config.prompt: 'Get fitter' is too vague to program — file the components:
config.why: Specificity: each component adapts to its own stimulus — long slow running buys endurance and barely touches strength; heavy squatting buys strength and barely touches VO₂max.

activities.caption: pair the protocol with the component it measures
activities.name: tlaProtoMatch

config.prompt: Match each field protocol to the component it estimates:
config.why: A test is meaningful only if it is valid (measures the component it claims to) and reliable (same conditions, same result).
